title: After watching an AI burn $1,700 on game dev, I built a $0 Playbook for making complete games using only free web chats (7 Modules, 3 Layers & 10 Critic Lenses)
author: Maksim_Volganin_11
selftext:
The $0 AI Game Dev Playbook: How to Build Complete 2D/3D Games Using Only Free Web Chats (Without Losing Your Mind) Recently, I watched a massive AI game-dev experiment where autonomous coding agents (like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex) built 27 game versions across 76 hours, racking up over $1,700 in theoretical API costs. The findings were eye-opening—not just for people with huge API budgets, but especially for solo devs like me who build games in free browser-based AI chats (like Google Search AI / Gemini, free ChatGPT, or Claude web). When you use free web chats, you don't have autonomous agents running terminal loops, taking screenshots, or editing your files directly. You have a single chat window, a context limit, and a fast model that loves to take shortcuts, hallucinate variable names, or break working code the moment your script passes 800 lines. Over the past few months, I’ve systematized a strict Human-in-the-Loop Orchestration Pipeline that brings the power of multi-agent workflows into free web chats. It works universally for 2D (Phaser 3) and 3D (Godot 4), eliminates spaghetti code, and lets you ship polished, playable web games for $0. Here is the complete, step-by-step blueprint and prompt library I use.

# 1. The Core Philosophy: Why Free AI Chats Fail (And How to Fix It)

In the $1,700 experiment, three fatal flaws emerged when letting AI build games unchecked:

1. The "Weak Draft" Trap: If you ask a fast/free model to write a rough draft of a whole game, it builds terrible core logic and broken balance. Even if you polish it later, the foundation remains rotten.
2. Context Amnesia: Once a single script grows past 800–1,000 lines, a free chat forgets how it named a function at the top of the file.
3. Endless Blind Polishing: Asking an AI to "make it better" causes it to fix one bug while inventing two new ones.

The Solution: You act as the Lead Architect & Producer. The AI never builds the whole game at once. Instead, you divide the project into 7 tiny, isolated modules, push the entire game through 3 distinct development Layers, and rotate 4 specialized AI personas across fresh chat tabs.

# 2. Workspace Setup: The Solo Dev Command Center

Before writing a single line of code, set up three free tools to prevent data loss and context drift:

1. AI Notebooks (e.g., Google AI Mode Notebooks / NotebookLM): Create one dedicated Notebook per game. Upload your 1-page Pitch, Module Map, and "STATE.md" as Sources. Every new chat tab you open inside this Notebook automatically inherits your project rules without you re-pasting them.
2. Local Version Control (GitHub Desktop): Free AI will eventually give you a snippet that breaks everything. Commit your working project before applying any major AI suggestion. If it breaks, revert in 2 seconds.
3. The Living Anchor ("STATE.md"): Keep a 30-line Markdown file in your project root and Notebook Sources. It tracks which modules are done, what signals exist, and what the immediate next step is.

Master System Instruction (Paste into your AI Notebook Settings): You are a Senior Game Developer and Technical Architect.

* Engine: \[Godot 4.3 (GDScript) / Phaser 3 (ES6 Modules)\].
* Architecture: Strict modular design. Never write monolithic files. Keep scripts under 250 lines.
* Decoupling: Modules must NEVER call each other directly. Communicate strictly via \[Godot Signals / Phaser EventEmitter\] and a global GameManager/EventBus.
* Visual Separation: Always separate physical hitboxes/logic from visual sprites/meshes so placeholders can be swapped for real assets later without touching gameplay code.
* Config-Driven Balance: Never hardcode magic numbers (speeds, timers, damage, spawn rates). Expose all balance levers at the top of the script via \[@export variables / a central Config.js file\].
* Web & Mobile Ready: All controls must support both Mouse/Keyboard and Touch (tap/drag/swipe) seamlessly. UI must scale cleanly on both 16:9 desktop and 9:16 mobile viewports.

# 3. The Universal 7-Module Architecture

Whether you are building a hyper-casual 2D arcade game in Phaser 3 or an isometric 3D prototype in Godot 4, every small-to-medium game fits into these 7 isolated files:

1. Brain / State ("GameManager.gd" Autoload in Godot / "GameState.js" EventBus in Phaser): Score, high score, game states ("MENU", "PLAY", "GAMEOVER"), speed multiplier, and global signals.
2. World / Arena ("Arena.gd" + "WorldEnvironment" in Godot / "MainScene.js" in Phaser): Camera setup, lighting, background/scrolling floor, and screen boundaries.
3. Player / Actor ("Actor.gd" in Godot / "Player.js" in Phaser): Player movement physics, input handling (tap/click/keys), hitbox, and visual container.
4. Spawner ("Spawner.gd" in Godot / "Spawner.js" in Phaser): Procedural generation of obstacles, enemies, coins, or platforms plus the difficulty scaling curve.
5. Rules & Combat ("Rules.gd" in Godot / "CollisionManager.js" in Phaser): Hit detection, combo multipliers, damage, win/loss triggers, and risk-reward logic.
6. Interface / UI ("UI.gd" CanvasLayer in Godot / "UIScene.js" in Phaser): Minimalist HUD: Title overlay, live score/combo counter, and Game Over screen with instant restart.
7. Game Feel / Juice ("Juice.gd" in Godot / "JuiceManager.js" in Phaser): Hitstop (freeze frames), screen shake, particle bursts, Tween squash-and-stretch animations, and procedural SFX.

# 4. The 3-Layer Production Pipeline

Golden Rule: Never polish one module to 100% before building the others. Push the entire 7-module skeleton through Layer 1 first, then upgrade the whole game to Layer 2, and finally Layer 3.

# LAYER 1: The Greybox Skeleton (Gameplay on Primitives)

Goal: Prove the game is fun using ugly rectangles (Phaser) or cubes/capsules (Godot). Zero custom art.

* Step 1 — Ideation & The 1-Page Pitch (Creator Chat): Avoid generic prompts like "give me a game idea." Use constraints, genre-blending, and the "3-Second Hook" rule (the player must understand how to play from a single screenshot with zero tutorial text).
* Step 2 — Module & Signal Blueprint (Architect Chat): Lock down the exact names of your 7 files and their signals. Save this as "BLUEPRINT.md" in your Notebook.
* Step 3 — Module-by-Module Coding (Executor Chats): Open a fresh chat for every 1–2 modules. Force the AI to think through edge cases before generating code. Assemble the greybox game in your engine until you can play from Start to Game Over.
* Step 4 — Logic Audit & Human Playtest (Critic Chat + Live Test): Run 3–4 Critic Lenses on your code. Then, sit a friend down in front of the greybox game without saying a single word. Watch where they get confused in the first 30 seconds.

# LAYER 2: The Art Pipeline (Procedural + Free AI Assets)

Goal: Replace greybox shapes with cohesive visuals and snappy animations without breaking your working physics.

* Path A — Procedural Geometry & Shaders (Best for 3D Godot): In 3D, lighting, shadows, and perspective make primitive shapes (cylinders, cones, spheres) look like charming tabletop miniatures. Ask the Executor to write "@tool" scripts that assemble buildings, vehicles, or stylized animals from primitives, paired with "WorldEnvironment" fog/glow.
* Path B — External AI Assets (2D Sprites or Tripo/Meshy 3D):

1. Open an Art Director Chat to lock down a strict visual bible (color palette, lighting angle, outline thickness) so your assets don't look like a random collage. 2. Generate static sprites on transparent backgrounds (2D) or neutral-pose ".glb" meshes via free tiers of Tripo AI / Meshy AI (3D). 3. Skip AI sprite-sheets and AI auto-rigging: They are notoriously buggy. Instead, animate static sprites and 3D meshes in code using Tween squash-and-stretch, sinusoidal bobbing, and wheel/turret rotation.

# LAYER 3: Game Feel ("Juice"), Audio & Retention Tuning

Goal: Transform a "working prototype" into an addictive, tactile experience.

* Micro-Meta Progression: Add a lightweight loop between runs—such as unlocking new visual skins or picking 1 of 3 random rogue-lite upgrades every 30 seconds.
* Procedural & Pitch-Shifted Audio: Sound is 50% of game feel. In Phaser 3, ask the AI to synthesize retro sound effects directly via the browser's Web Audio API (zero ".mp3" files needed). In Godot, increase "pitch\_scale" dynamically with each consecutive combo hit to trigger a strong dopamine loop.
* The "Juice" Module: Wire up screen shake, hitstop (a 40ms pause on heavy impacts), and particle bursts to your existing signals.

# 5. Copy-Paste Prompt Library (The 4 Chat Personas)

Never mix roles in a single chat window. When a chat gets long or starts repeating mistakes, open a fresh tab and paste the corresponding template below. Persona 1: The Anti-Cliché Creator (Brainstorming) Act as a Lead Game Designer specializing in high-retention web and hyper-casual games (like YouTube Playables, Poki, and Voodoo hits). I am building a \[2D game in Phaser 3 / 3D isometric game in Godot 4\]. Generate 10 distinct game concepts. STRICT CONSTRAINTS:

1. Ban all clichés: NO standard endless runners, NO basic match-3, NO generic space shooters, NO clickers.
2. Use the "Familiar + Unexpected" setting formula (e.g., instead of "zombie shooter," use "pizza delivery driver during an alien invasion").
3. The core mechanic must pass the "3-Second Hook" test: understandable from a single screenshot with ZERO text tutorials.
4. Controls must use at most 1–2 inputs (click/tap, hold, or drag) that feel equally great on mouse and mobile touch.

For each concept, output:

* Title & High-Concept Pitch (1 sentence)
* The 10-Second Core Loop
* The "Risk vs. Reward" greed mechanic (how players risk failure for double points)
* 4 Balance Levers (@export / Config variables)

Persona 2: The System Architect (Creating the Blueprint) Act as a Principal Game Architect. Based on our approved 1-Page Pitch, design the technical blueprint for our 7-module architecture:

1. GameManager (State & Signals)
2. Arena (World, Camera, Lighting)
3. Actor (Player physics & input)
4. Spawner (Obstacles, enemies, difficulty curve)
5. Rules (Collisions, scoring, combos, win/loss)
6. UI (HUD, Start, Game Over)
7. Juice (Particles, camera shake, tweens, audio)

Do NOT write full game code yet. Output a clean Markdown specification ("BLUEPRINT.md") containing:

* Exact file names and node/class hierarchy.
* Every global Signal/Event name and the exact arguments it passes.
* The exact list of balance variables to place in our Config.
* Placeholder hitbox dimensions (in pixels or 3D units) so we can build Layer 1 on primitives.

Persona 3: The Disciplined Executor (Writing Module Code) Act as a Senior \[Godot 4 / Phaser 3\] Developer. Refer to "BLUEPRINT.md" in our Notebook sources. Today we are building ONLY Module #\[X\]: "\[FileName\]". CRITICAL INSTRUCTIONS:

1. Do NOT write code immediately. First, write a brief step-by-step logic plan for this module and list 3 edge cases (e.g., double-tapping restart, objects spawning off-screen, null references) and how you will prevent them.
2. Keep the code under 250 lines, clean, and well-commented.
3. Use primitive shapes (rectangles/circles or CSG boxes/capsules) for visuals right now, attached to a separate visual container node so we can swap in real art on Layer 2.
4. Connect to other modules ONLY using the exact Signals/Events defined in "BLUEPRINT.md".

Persona 4: The Art Director (Layer 2 Asset Prompts) Act as an Indie Game Art Director. Review "BLUEPRINT.md" and our current Layer 1 prototype. We are moving to Layer 2 (Visuals). Create an Art Bible and asset generation prompts:

1. Define a cohesive color palette (4–5 hex codes: background, foreground, player, hazards, collectibles) ensuring high contrast so gameplay elements pop instantly.
2. Specify which elements should be built procedurally via code/shaders vs. generated as external assets.
3. Write ready-to-use English prompts for \[2D Image Generator / Tripo AI & Meshy AI 3D\] for each hero asset. Enforce a consistent style, neutral/top-down/isometric camera angle matching our game, and clean silhouettes with no messy small details.
4. Suggest 3 simple code-driven Tween animations (scale, rotation, bobbing) to bring these static assets to life without needing complex skeletal rigs or sprite sheets.

# 6. The 10 "Critic Lenses" (How to Run Deep Audits Without Breaking Code)

If you open a new chat and simply say "Review my code and improve it," the AI will give generic praise or invent unnecessary rewrites. Instead, run targeted passes in fresh chat tabs using specific Critic Lenses—forcing the model into deep analytical reasoning from a single angle at a time.

# Phase A: Design & Balance Lenses (Use on your 1-Page Pitch before coding)

1. The Boredom Killer (First 15 Seconds): "Analyze this pitch purely for player retention in the first 15 seconds. Where is the slowest, most boring moment where a browser player would close the tab? Propose 3 ways to make the opening second instant action."
2. The Exploit & Cheater Lens: "Act like a player trying to break this game's rules. How can someone spam one input, camp in one corner, or hoard a resource to get infinite points with zero skill? Adjust the rules to close these loopholes."
3. The Flow & Difficulty Curve Lens: "Simulate a player's experience at 30 seconds, 2 minutes, and 5 minutes. Where does the game become either too easy (boredom) or an unfair brick wall (frustration)? Write a mathematical formula for smooth difficulty scaling."
4. The Greed / Risk-Reward Lens: "Evaluate whether players have a meaningful 'push your luck' decision every few seconds. If not, design a risk-reward mechanic that uses our existing controls without adding new buttons."
5. The Procedural Feasibility Lens: "Review this concept as a technical artist. Which visual elements will look terrible if built with simple primitives or cheap AI assets? Replace weak visual ideas with elements that shine using geometric shapes, particles, and lighting."

# Phase B: Code & Architecture Lenses (Use after Layer 1 and Layer 3)

1. The Decoupling Audit: "Check these scripts for tight coupling. Where is one module directly accessing internal variables of another? Refactor those interactions into clean Signals/Events so any module can be disabled without crashing the game."
2. The Compiler Crash-Test: "Step through this code line-by-line like a strict compiler. Simulate 5 edge cases: mashing restart mid-animation, colliding with two hazards on the exact same frame, division by zero, and unloaded nodes. Point out every potential crash or Null Reference."
3. The FPS & Memory Leak Hunter: "Audit this code for web and mobile performance. Identify heavy loops inside "\_process" / "update()", unfreed objects ("queue\_free" / object pooling), and redundant allocations that will cause stutter in browser builds."
4. The Tactile "Game Feel" Lens: "Inspect the input, collision, and scoring code. Pinpoint the exact lines where player actions feel 'floaty' or unresponsive, and specify where to trigger hitstop, camera shake, pitch-shifted audio, and Tween curves."
5. The Config & Maintainability Pass: "Find every hardcoded number left inside the logic functions (speeds, cooldowns, health, shake intensity) and extract them into cleanly commented "@export" / "Config.js" parameters for rapid live tuning."

# 7. Quick-Start Checklist for a Weekend Game Jam

If you want to test this entire workflow over a single weekend:

* Friday Evening (2 hours): Create your AI Notebook -> Run Creator + 3 Design Lenses -> Lock in "BLUEPRINT.md".
* Saturday (5–6 hours): Build all 7 modules on Layer 1 (primitives) -> Run Compiler Crash-Test & Decoupling Audit -> Do a silent 5-minute playtest with a friend.
* Sunday Morning (3 hours): Layer 2 Art Pass (Art Director prompts -> swap in procedural 3D/sprites + Tween animations).
* Sunday Afternoon (3 hours): Layer 3 Polish ("Juice" module + Web Audio / pitch-shifted SFX + Config balance tuning) -> Export HTML5 build.

# Want to Test This Pipeline in a Chill Weekend Jam?

If you enjoy experimenting with free AI tools to make small, polished games without spending a dime on subscriptions or paid APIs, I’m hosting a laid-back, 4-day community jam starting next Friday (December 4 – December 7, 2026). There are no strict themes, no elitism, and no paid tools allowed—just solo devs, free AI chats, and creative 2D/web experiments. You can find it on itch io by searching for: "Cozy AI 2D Sandbox ($0 Tools)" (Bonus challenge: in your game description, share 1 or 2 of the funniest prompts or weirdest AI hallucinations you ran into while building it!) If you try out this 7-module / 3-layer workflow on your next prototype, let me know how it goes or what tweaks you’d make to the Critic Lenses!
